title: "`LazyFrame`s"
---

```{python}
#| label: setup-lazyframes
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: every example on this page uses these imports"
#| output: false
import polars as pl

import dagster_dataframely as dd
from dagster_dataframely.data import OrdersSchema
```

Annotate an input as `pl.LazyFrame` under `PolarsParquetIOManager`, and Polars drops the rows and columns your plan does not need while it reads the file.
Return a `pl.LazyFrame`, and the package collects your whole plan once, on Polars' streaming engine.

<!-- rumdl-disable-next-line MD078 -->

```{mermaid}
        V5 --> V6["DataFrame passed to the IO manager"]

```

## Reading an input as a `LazyFrame`

Annotate an input as `pl.LazyFrame`, and the IO manager returns a scan that has not run yet.
Polars then pushes a `filter` or `select` down into the scan, so it drops those rows and columns while it reads the file:

```{python}
#| label: lazyframes-1
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)
def recent(orders: pl.LazyFrame) -> pl.LazyFrame:
    return orders.filter(pl.col("amount") > 100)
```

The IO manager reads the input, not this package, so the annotation works the same on a plain `@dg.asset`.
A pickling IO manager such as `dg.FilesystemIOManager` returns the `pl.DataFrame` the upstream asset wrote.
Dagster then fails the step with `DagsterTypeCheckDidNotPass` for a `pl.LazyFrame` annotation.
Annotate `pl.DataFrame` instead and the IO manager reads the whole file.

## Validation collects the plan

`Schema.filter` takes a plan and returns two: one for the valid rows and one for the invalid rows.
This package collects both in one `collect_all` call on the streaming engine, so Polars reads the source once.

```{python}
#| label: lazyframes-2
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)
def orders(raw_orders: pl.LazyFrame) -> pl.LazyFrame:
    return raw_orders.filter(pl.col("amount") > 0)
```

So your joins, filters and aggregations run on the streaming engine.
Polars falls back to the in-memory engine for any operation the streaming engine does not support, so the engine choice never makes a plan fail.

The streaming engine processes the plan in batches, so it does not hold every intermediate row in memory at once.
Peak memory includes the plan's output and one boolean column per rule, held once while `Schema.filter` separates the valid rows from the invalid rows.
This helps a plan with a large intermediate result, such as a join that multiplies rows before a filter removes most of them.
The in-memory engine would hold every row that join produced.
A returned `DataFrame` goes through the same call after `.lazy()`, which copies no data.
The column-schema check runs first and reads only `collect_schema()`, which does not run the plan.
So the package raises `ColumnSchemaError` for a frame whose columns or dtypes differ from the schema's, before the plan runs.

## The IO manager receives a `DataFrame`

The plan runs on the streaming engine, but the write does not stream: the IO manager receives a `DataFrame` in memory.
The package counts the valid rows and the invalid rows before it writes the asset's table, because a run that raises `ValidationAbortError` or `NoValidRowsError` does not write it.
A plain `@dg.asset` has no validation, checks or statistics, so it can stream end to end without collecting its result into memory.
The measurements are in [`docs/pre-1.0.md`](https://github.com/ozanozbeker/dagster-dataframely/blob/main/docs/pre-1.0.md#lazy-validation-and-lazy-storage).

Schema on write needs the result in memory, so it suits silver and gold tables better than data at ingestion scale.
